extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction writers, and students of the craft of fiction (literary critics/teachers)
extracted.subtask_short: novel writing: method & point of view
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting and executing narrative method (pictorial vs scenic), managing point of view, preparing effects, and shaping time, climax, and character in long fiction (novels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary pictorial preparation (Balzac's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay out a full, enduring picture of the setting and lives of the characters in advance so the later action can be told concisely and still carry a full sense of history and time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balzac 'amasses in his opening picture the reserve of effect that he needs.' By creating a detailed tableau (house, furniture, routine, social position) the writer provides material that can later be 'destroyed' or invoked to show decay, change, or duration without lengthy intermediate treatment (examples: Eugenie Grandet, La Recherche de l'Absolu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create the sense of time through scene and setting, not only by statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Secure the representation of time in the preliminary picture so that later statements like 'Five years went by' carry the impression of gradual fading or change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than relying on explicit summaries of duration, prepare the reader with a thorough depiction of routine, sameness, and accumulating days so the passing years are 'divined and accepted at once.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of preparation; reserve of effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Work by forestalling and anticipating: create and hold effects in advance so that when needed they can be used without ostentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer 'makes a point and reserves it at the same time' — the art is to hold an effect back until its due page. This economy increases the force of the climax and avoids laborious expatiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax's proper role — complete and make book organic
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax ought only to 'complete, to add the touch that makes the book whole and organic; that is its task, and that only.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not burden the climax with required preparation or subordinate tasks; save for the climax only the movement or touch that declares and fulfils the book's intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hinging the story on sudden, implausible revelations
rubrics_metrics.description: Realistic disappointments and final collapses often 'steal into a life' rather than fall as a stroke; avoid making the book hinge on a single abrupt discovery when the truth is gradual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a climax that is pictorial and gradual (e.g., the slow chill descending on Eugenie) rather than an over-dramatized single incident; treat the 'final act' as coda if the drama is already essentially complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and intensification as structural device
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject requires iterated failures or outbreaks (a fixed idea developing by repeated incidents), structure the book as a sustained movement that reiterates the same effect with growing intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balzac's La Recherche shows how a richly furnished opening scene provides 'plenty to destroy,' so that successive repetitions of failure regain force because the prepared scene grows more ravaged and the effect deepens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose scene-based (dramatic) vs pictorial method according to the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the material calls for immediate scenic presentation (Tolstoy) or for a general pictorial impression and retrospective preparation (Balzac).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy treats material 'scenically' — chain of particular occasions with exact hour and place — while Balzac prefers broad pictorial preface. The method should 'arise out of the subject' rather than be merely the author's congenial habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic immediacy (Tolstoy's dramatic plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the story as a sequence of fully realized scenes, each defined in time and place, making the reader watch characters by direct vision rather than through generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strict dramatic plan allows continual immediacy and many episodes; the author may still enter characters' minds when needed, but the dominant mode is action and scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing exterior scene with interior consciousness where effective
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in a scenic method, freely 'lay bare the mind of any of his people' when it helps force or lucidity; combine external action with quick interior glimpses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy's method is 'mixed' — largely scenic but with light, quick entries into consciousness to give characters private reality without losing scenic rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create character either by comprehensive picture or by dramatic scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac tends to create people by a broad, methodical picture of their world and history; Tolstoy often creates them within the movement of scenes and passing episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the approach that suits your material: a 'Holbein-picture' of background supports a long, pictorial novel; vivid half-page scenes can create immediate, memorable character with small means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method must arise from the subject (not the author's habitual method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not impose a favored technique on matter unsuited to it; Tolstoy's scenic fidelity harmed Anna Karenina's opening because the subject required a concentrated preparation which his method refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether your story needs pictorial preparation or scenic unfolding and let that requirement determine point-of-view choices and structural packing of early material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate preparation before a character's pivotal action
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the reader has sufficient knowledge of a character's past, situation, and inward life before that character is required to act at a critical emotional height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anna's fall feels abrupt because Tolstoy did not tightly pack the opening to show 'all Anna's past and present' at once; either compress the opening into a concentrated picture or delay the crisis until the character is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small vivid scenes to enrich and enlarge character
rubrics_metrics.description: Brief, sharply observed episodes (half-page scenes) can become 'part of them' and add eloquent memory and depth to characters without being mere diversions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy's flashes — a child teasing a servant, a peasant in a doorway — speed the story by augmenting tone and contributing to a character's fullness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art of preparation must be unobtrusive
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of preparation 'is no art if it betrays itself at the outset' — good preparation should be unrecognizable until its effect is realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obvious or self-conscious devices that call attention to the craft; the readiness of the climax depends on preparations that evade detection until they pay off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid handling the stroke tactlessly or obtrusively
rubrics_metrics.description: If the preparatory stroke is 'handled tactlessly and obtrusively' the pleasure and effectiveness of the climax are spoiled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain subtlety and restraint; the reader should re-perceive the stroke with satisfaction, not feel manipulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift of point-of-view / dramatization through a spokesman
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing a recognizable narrator or 'spokesman' dramatizes the author's presence and shifts responsibility onto a visible voice inside the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the author's assertion risks seeming arbitrary, setting up a spokesman 'in the story himself' gives authority, discloses relation to material, and makes the tale self-contained.

rubrics_metrics.name: If the story examines the narrator's consciousness, show the mind at work
rubrics_metrics.description: When the narrator is himself the subject, an after-the-fact report is less powerful than scenes showing his mind in agitation and operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer immediate presentation of mental activity rather than retrospective chronicle when the point is to explore consciousness; accomplish this by further shifts of point-of-view to place the reader nearer the moment of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not leave essential exposition until the climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Important understanding required for the climax should not be postponed; the climax must not be expected to do what the earlier book has failed to accomplish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the beginnings must make a complex situation clear, use the method that most condenses and concentrates representation so that later action is intelligible and meaningful.
